title: Build Your Own Robot Friend: An Open-Source Learning Module for Accessible and Engaging AI Education
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of making AI education more accessible, affordable, and engaging for learners from different socio-economic backgrounds. The authors argue that many existing AI and robotics education tools are either too expensive, too closed and inflexible, or too narrowly focused on technical content without covering human-centered AI topics such as human-robot interaction, affective computing, and AI ethics. The paper therefore asks whether an open-source, low-cost, customizable learning module centered on building a social robot can provide an effective and engaging introduction to AI, machine learning, and robotics.

The intervention is a three-part open-source learning module built around a simplified version of the Blossom social robot. Part 1 teaches students to assemble and program their own robot using redesigned 3D-printable hardware and customizable exterior designs. Part 2 introduces a human-centered machine learning pipeline, including training a smiling-classification model on the CelebA dataset and discussing algorithmic fairness and AI ethics. Part 3 integrates robot control with OpenSense so that students program the robot to recognize and imitate user head movements. The robot was redesigned to reduce fabrication complexity and cost, with the authors reporting that each robot can cost under $250 when parts are printed at scale or in-house.

The empirical evaluation focused on a two-day in-person workshop conducted at a single minority-serving institution in the United States. Fifteen college students participated, and 13 completed the post-workshop survey. Because of workshop time constraints, only Parts 1 and 3 of the module were evaluated in practice. The context was hands-on, in-person team-based work where participants built and programmed the robot over two days. The broader intended audience for the module includes both college and high school students, but the actual evaluated sample was undergraduate students.

The main conclusions are that the module was perceived by participants as effective, easy to follow, and engaging, and that it increased their interest in studying AI and robotics in the future. All teams successfully completed the workshop tasks, and post-workshop survey results were strongly favorable across perceived learning in robotics, software engineering, AI/ML, and mechanical engineering. At the same time, the evidence is limited to short-term usability and self-reported perceptions from a small sample at one institution, and the authors note that future work should evaluate the machine learning/ethics portion and test the module with high school students.

identified_tools.name: Blossom
identified_tools.description: An open-source socially expressive robot platform adapted here into a simplified, affordable, customizable educational robot for hands-on AI/ML, robotics, and human-centered AI learning.
identified_tools.use_case: Students built and programmed a modified Blossom robot in a two-day workshop, including assembling hardware and completing a human-robot interaction program where the robot recognized and imitated users’ head movements.

findings.finding_summary: In a two-day usability workshop, 92% of surveyed participants reported that the module helped them learn more about robotics/electronic engineering, computer science/software engineering, AI/ML, and mechanical engineering. Post-workshop Likert responses were significantly above neutral: robotics/electronic engineering (median = Strongly Agree (2), p = .0004), computer science/software engineering (median = Strongly Agree (2), p = .0008), AI/ML (median = Strongly Agree (2), p = .0014), and mechanical engineering (median = Strongly Agree (2), p = .0018).
findings.measure: Post-workshop 5-point Likert survey of perceived learning gains across robotics/electronic engineering, computer science/software engineering, AI/ML, and mechanical engineering

findings.finding_summary: The learning module was perceived as easy to follow by 85% of participants who completed the post-workshop survey. Responses were significantly more favorable than neutral on a 5-point Likert scale (median = Strongly Agree (2), p = .0009).
findings.measure: Post-workshop 5-point Likert survey of perceived usability/ease-of-following

findings.finding_summary: All four teams successfully completed the workshop goals, and 100% of surveyed participants reported that the workshop encouraged them to study more robotics and AI in the future. The corresponding Likert response was significantly above neutral (median = Strongly Agree (2), p = .0001).
findings.measure: Workshop task completion and post-workshop 5-point Likert survey of future interest in studying robotics and AI

quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-sample usability workshop with post-survey and qualitative feedback, not an RCT or quasi-experimental effectiveness study. Findings rely primarily on student self-reports from 13 survey respondents.
impact_tier_rationale: Results are uniformly positive, but impact is based on perceived learning, usability, and interest rather than standardized learning gains, and no effect sizes are reported.
